subject: Mixed
description: Medium-difficulty practice set (20 questions) covering: Anatomy, Fundamentals of Electro Therapy, General Surgery & Orthopedics, Kinesio Therapeutics, OBGY, Pathology & Microbiology, Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills, Physiology, Physiotherapy in Community Health, Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition, Physiotherapy in Neurosciences.

questions.question: A woman who delivers twins in her first pregnancy is correctly recorded as:

options.A: Gravida 2, Para 2
options.B: Gravida 1, Para 1
options.C: Gravida 2, Para 1

questions.explanation: Gravida and para refer to PREGNANCIES, not the number of babies delivered. A woman delivering twins in her first pregnancy is still gravida one, para one — parity is not increased by multiple fetuses in a single pregnancy.
questions.sourceChapter: Antenatal Care — History Taking, Vital Statistics
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Liquefactive (colliquative) necrosis, seen classically in cerebral infarcts and abscess cavities, occurs because:

options.A: Calcium soaps form and harden the tissue
options.B: Hydrolytic enzymes play a dominant role in tissue degradation, producing semi-fluid material
options.C: The tissue is replaced entirely by fibrous scar with no enzymatic activity
options.D: Granulomatous inflammation surrounds a cheese-like centre

questions.explanation: Liquefactive necrosis occurs commonly from ischaemic injury or bacterial/fungal infection, where hydrolytic enzymes dominate tissue degradation, converting the affected area into semi-fluid material — classic examples are a brain infarct and an abscess cavity.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Liquefaction Necrosis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: At what approximate stimulation frequency does a muscle contraction become fully tetanic, with no perceptible relaxation between successive contractions?

options.A: Over 60 Hz
options.B: Under 1 Hz
options.C: Exactly 10 Hz
options.D: Frequency has no relationship to tetany

questions.explanation: As stimulation frequency increases beyond 20 Hz, partial tetany develops; further increases progressively reduce relaxation until, at frequencies over 60 Hz, there is no perceptible relaxation between contractions and the response is fully tetanic.
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Frequency of Stimulation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Closed-chain exercise is best described as exercise performed:

options.A: In a nonweight-bearing position with the distal segment moving freely
options.B: In a weight-bearing position where the body moves over a fixed distal segment
options.C: Only using free weights, never body weight

questions.explanation: Closed-chain exercise is performed in a weight-bearing position, where the body moves over a relatively fixed distal segment (e.g. the foot on the ground during a squat). Open-chain exercise, by contrast, is performed nonweight-bearing, with the distal segment (hand or foot) moving freely.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Position for Exercise
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: The Hawkins-Kennedy impingement test involves forward flexing the arm to 90° and then forcibly:

options.A: Medially rotating the shoulder
options.B: Laterally rotating the shoulder only
options.C: Extending the elbow fully

questions.explanation: In the Hawkins-Kennedy test, the examiner forward flexes the arm to 90° and then forcibly medially rotates the shoulder, pushing the supraspinatus tendon against the coracoacromial ligament and coracoid process — pain indicates a positive test for supraspinatus tendinosis or impingement.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Hawkins-Kennedy Impingement Test
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Blastomas (embryomas) such as neuroblastoma, nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour), and retinoblastoma are notable because they:

options.A: Occur almost exclusively in adults over 60
options.B: Arise from embryonal/partially differentiated cells and occur more frequently in infants and children under 5
options.C: Are always benign despite the '-oma' name

questions.explanation: Blastomas arise from embryonal or partially differentiated cells that would normally form the blastema of organs/tissues during embryogenesis, and occur more frequently in infants and children under 5 years of age.
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Special Categories of Tumours
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: The basic requirements of good epidemiological measurement include validity, reliability, accuracy, sensitivity, and:

options.A: Specificity
options.B: Profitability
options.C: Popularity among clinicians
options.D: Simplicity above all else, regardless of accuracy

questions.explanation: The basic requirements of measurement in epidemiology are validity, reliability, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity — these properties determine how trustworthy and useful a given measurement or test is for epidemiological purposes.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods — Basic Measurements in Epidemiology
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: For the vertebroscapular muscles (e.g., the rhomboids), resistance is preferably applied on the arm rather than directly on the scapula, their true point of insertion. Why?

options.A: It is simply easier for the therapist to grip the arm
options.B: The longer lever at the arm better reflects the functional demand of controlling the weight of the whole upper limb
options.C: The scapula moves too unpredictably to resist against
options.D: Resistance at the scapula risks skin breakdown

questions.explanation: Applying resistance on the arm uses a longer lever that more closely reflects the functional load these muscles must control (the weight of the arm), rather than testing at their literal anatomical insertion.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Madelung's deformity results from retarded growth of which structure?

options.A: The lower end of the radius
options.B: The upper end of the humerus
options.C: The olecranon process of the ulna

questions.explanation: Madelung's deformity is a dorsal subluxation (displacement) of the lower end of the ulna, caused by retarded growth of the lower end of the radius.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: On the International Death Certificate, the 'underlying cause of death' is recorded in Part I, and is defined as:

options.A: The immediate mode of dying, such as 'heart failure' or 'asthenia'
options.B: The disease or injury that initiated the chain of morbid events leading directly to death, or the circumstances of the accident/violence that produced the fatal injury
options.C: Any condition present at death regardless of its role in causing it
options.D: Only conditions diagnosed after an autopsy

questions.explanation: The underlying cause of death is the disease or injury that initiated the train of morbid events leading directly to death, or the circumstances of the accident/violence producing the fatal injury — the certificate explicitly notes this does NOT mean the immediate mode of dying (e.g. 'heart failure' or 'asthenia' are not acceptable as the underlying cause).
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — International Death Certificate
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Mortality statistics are described as 'virtually useless' for studying which category of disease?

options.A: Diseases with very high fatality rates
options.B: Diseases with low fatality, such as mental diseases or arthritis
options.C: All infectious diseases without exception

questions.explanation: Mortality data are virtually useless for studying diseases associated with low fatality, such as mental diseases or arthritis, since these conditions rarely appear as a cause of death even though they cause significant morbidity — morbidity data are needed instead for such conditions.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — Limitations of Mortality Data
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Idiopathic (hereditary) haemochromatosis is characterised by a classic triad of pigmentary liver cirrhosis, skin pigmentation, and:

options.A: Pancreatic damage resulting in diabetes mellitus ('bronze diabetes')
options.B: Complete loss of vision
options.C: Chronic renal failure exclusively

questions.explanation: Hereditary haemochromatosis is characterised by a triad: pigmentary liver cirrhosis, pancreatic damage causing diabetes mellitus, and skin pigmentation — earning it the nickname 'bronze diabetes' based on the latter two features.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Pigments, Haemosiderin
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: A Grade 3 (third-degree) soft tissue injury is characterised by:

options.A: Mild pain only within the first 24 hours, with minimal swelling
options.B: Near-complete or complete tear/avulsion of the tissue, often with instability if a ligament is involved, and stress to the tissue being usually painless
options.C: Moderate pain requiring the activity to stop, with some fibers torn
options.D: No pain whatsoever, at any point

questions.explanation: A Grade 3 injury involves near-complete or complete tear/avulsion of the tissue (tendon or ligament); notably, stress to the injured tissue is usually painless (since it's fully torn), and a torn ligament results in joint instability — a key distinguishing feature from Grade 1 and 2 injuries.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 10: Soft Tissue Injury, Repair, and Management — Severity of Tissue Injury
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Why is serum albumin considered an unreliable direct measure of a patient's nutritional status, especially in the acute setting?

options.A: Albumin levels never change regardless of nutrition or illness
options.B: Hypoalbuminaemia often results from altered body fluid composition and increased capillary permeability related to sepsis, not nutrition alone
options.C: Albumin can only be measured once per year
options.D: Albumin is only produced by the kidneys, unrelated to nutrition

questions.explanation: Although a low serum albumin (<30 g/L) is a poor prognostic indicator, hypoalbuminaemia is frequently driven by alterations in body fluid composition and increased capillary permeability from ongoing sepsis or illness — not purely by nutritional intake — so albumin is not a reliable direct marker of nutritional status, particularly acutely.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutritional Assessment — Laboratory Techniques
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) syndrome classically produces contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss that is:

options.A: Greater in the lower extremity than the upper extremity
options.B: Greater in the upper extremity and face than the lower extremity
options.C: Equal throughout the whole body with no distinguishing pattern

questions.explanation: Because the ACA supplies the medial aspect of the cerebral hemisphere where the lower extremity is somatotopically represented, ACA syndrome classically produces contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss with greater involvement of the lower extremity than the upper extremity — the opposite pattern to MCA syndrome.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Anterior Cerebral Artery Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: The Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) uses which three components to calculate overall risk of undernutrition?

options.A: BMI, recent weight loss, and the acute disease effect (likely absence of nutritional intake)
options.B: Blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature only
options.C: Age, gender, and occupation

questions.explanation: The MUST tool combines three scored components — BMI, percentage weight loss over 3-6 months, and the acute disease effect (adding points if there has been or will likely be little/no nutritional intake for 5+ days) — to classify overall undernutrition risk as low, medium, or high.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutritional Assessment — Clinical, The MUST Tool
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Cysticercosis in humans is most commonly acquired by:

options.A: Direct mosquito bite
options.B: Eating undercooked pork ('measly pork') or ingesting contaminated vegetables/food carrying Taenia solium eggs
options.C: Airborne droplet transmission

questions.explanation: Cysticercosis is infection by the larval stage of Taenia solium (the pork tapeworm). Humans acquire it by eating undercooked ('measly') pork containing larval cysts, by ingesting food/vegetables contaminated with eggs, or occasionally by autoinfection.
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Cysticercosis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Chronic amoebic ulcers of the colon are classically described by which shape, due to undermining of the ulcer margins by the trophozoite's lytic action?

options.A: Punched-out ulcer
options.B: Flask-shaped ulcer
options.C: Serpiginous ulcer

questions.explanation: Chronic amoebic ulcers are described as 'flask-shaped' because the lytic action of Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites undermines and enlarges the ulcer margins beneath a narrower surface opening, giving it a flask-like profile on cross-section.
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Amoebiasis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognised cause of thrombocytopenia (decreased platelet count)?

options.A: Splenectomy
options.B: Hypersplenism (overactivity of the spleen)
options.C: Administration of epinephrine causing splenic contraction

questions.explanation: Hypersplenism (an overactive spleen) is a cause of thrombocytopenia, along with bone marrow depression, certain viral infections (e.g. dengue, which particularly attacks platelets), and drug hypersensitivity. By contrast, splenectomy, epinephrine-induced splenic contraction, and trauma/surgery are causes of thrombocytosis (increased platelet count) — the opposite direction.
questions.sourceChapter: Platelets or Thrombocytes — Count and Variations
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: By definition, a transient ischemic attack (TIA) produces focal neurological deficits that:

options.A: Last longer than 24 hours with permanent residual damage
options.B: Do not last longer than 24 hours, with no evidence of residual brain damage afterward
options.C: Always progress to a completed stroke within 24 hours
options.D: Only ever affect vision, never motor function

questions.explanation: A TIA is a temporary interruption of blood supply producing focal neurological deficits lasting minutes to hours but, by definition, not longer than 24 hours, with no evidence of residual damage afterward. However, TIA is clinically significant as a warning sign — about 15% of strokes are preceded by a TIA, with the highest risk in the following 90 days.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Management Categories
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences
